title: Surveyor 3: Into the Lunar Night
subtitle: A lunar scout that bounced on landing, tested the soil for Apollo — and was visited by astronauts years later.

model.credit: Procedural 3D model (no official NASA GLB available)

cover.credit: Pete Conrad at Surveyor 3, Apollo 12 (AS12-48-7134) — NASA

intro: 20 APR 1967. Surveyor 3 is descending toward the Ocean of Storms.
Apollo needs to know one thing: will the ground hold a crewed lander?
You have one lunar day of sunlight. Then comes the lunar night.

events.title: The engine will not stop
telemetry: !! DESCENT RADAR: CONFUSED BY REFLECTIVE ROCKS
events.text: At about 4.3 metres up the engines should have cut off. They did not. Surveyor 3 touches down and bounces back up — 10 metres high.

choices.label: Let it settle — then check health before doing anything
choices.outcome: It bounces twice — 10 m, then 3 m — and settles on the third touchdown at 00:04:17 UT inside a 200-metre crater. Less than an hour later the first of 6,326 TV pictures arrives.

choices.label: Immediately command a full camera and sampler checkout while still bouncing
choices.outcome: Commands arrive while the lander is still hopping. Nothing useful happens, and you lose energy and confidence in the hardware.

fact.title: Radar can be fooled
fact.text: Highly reflective rocks confused Surveyor 3’s descent radar, so the main engine failed to cut off at about 4.3 m. Sensor confusion during landing later ended other missions too, such as HAKUTO-R in 2023.

events.discuss: Surveyor 3 bounced before landing. Why do landers need to know exactly when they touch the ground?

events.title: Will the ground hold Apollo?
events.text: For the first time a Surveyor carries a surface sampler — a little scoop on an arm. Engineers on Earth want to know how strong the lunar soil is.

choices.label: Dig trenches and run bearing and impact tests in front of the camera
choices.outcome: Surveyor 3 digs four trenches and makes four bearing tests and thirteen impact tests. Verdict: the soil is like wet sand, with a bearing strength of about 0.7 kg/cm² — solid enough for an Apollo Lunar Module.

choices.label: Skip the sampler and spend the energy on photographs only
choices.outcome: Beautiful pictures — but Apollo planners still do not know how much the ground can bear.

fact.title: Why the scoop mattered
fact.text: Surveyor 3’s sampler experiments let scientists conclude that the lunar surface could support the weight of an Apollo lunar module — key information for the crewed landings.

events.discuss: Why did engineers need to know how strong the lunar soil was before sending astronauts?

events.title: Sunset on the Ocean of Storms
events.text: Lunar night begins on 2 May. It will last about two Earth weeks. Surveyor 3 is solar-powered.

choices.label: Keep the link open until the last possible moment
choices.outcome: Last contact: 4 May 1967, two days after the lunar night began. Surveyor 3 never wakes up again.

source.label: NASA Science — Footpads and Footprints: Humans and Machine Meet on the Moon

events.discuss: A lunar night lasts about 14 Earth days. What happens to a spacecraft with no sunlight and no heater power?

real_end.title: Silent vigil
real_end.text: You matched the real mission. Surveyor 3 proved the Moon could hold Apollo. Then it waited, silent, for two and a half years — until two astronauts walked up to it.

battery.title: Out of power
battery.text: The batteries ran down before the work was done.

integrity.title: Hardware failure
integrity.text: The lander was damaged beyond use.

epilogue: 19 November 1969: Apollo 12’s Pete Conrad and Alan Bean land about 180 m away, walk to Surveyor 3 and bring its TV camera and soil scoop back to Earth to study how 2½ years on the Moon affected them.

timeline: Bounced twice, then landed in Oceanus Procellarum.
Four trenches dug; soil judged strong enough for Apollo.
Last contact, two days into the lunar night.
Apollo 12 astronauts visited and removed the camera and scoop.

where.state: Still standing in Surveyor crater, minus its camera and scoop. NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter has imaged it next to the Apollo 12 descent stage and the astronauts’ footpaths.

image.caption: Pete Conrad examines Surveyor 3’s TV camera before removing it; the Apollo 12 Lunar Module Intrepid stands in the background.

inside.title: What came home
inside.text: The camera, some cable and tubing, and the trenching scoop were returned to Earth and studied. Part of the scoop is displayed at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory.

source.label: NASA JPL — Surveyor 3 camera returned from the Moon
